messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] problem plotting recombination frequency by old scores when mapping
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] problem plotting recombination frequency by old scores when mapping
messages.body_plain:
markerlrt() can't be used to estimate recombination fractions; it just performs a general likelihood ratio test for association between genotypes at two markers.

If you want to plot rf vs lod, you need to use the est.rf() function first.

karl

> Hello,
>
> I am in the process of trying to create a de novo linkage map for an F2 population containing a mix of dominant and codominant markers (coded as such in the cross object), and have run into a problem when I try to plot the recombination frequencies versus the LOD scores.
>
> I want to use the markerlrt() function to calculate recombination frequencies (since I know there is likely to be seg. distortion in the population), but I've also tried using est.rf(). After using either one of these functions, I try the following code to the plot the recombination fraction versus the LOD score:
>
> rf= pull.rf(cross, what="rf")
> lod= pull.rf(cross, what="lod")
> plot(as.numeric(rf), as.numeric(lod), xlab="recombination fraction", ylab="LOD")
>
> but the resulting plot is a straight line, with identical values one each access, as if the LOD score is being plotted versus the LOD score (I don't think the rf is being plotted vs the rf because the values range from 0 to 120), or as if the rf values == the LOD values. I have no idea what's going on here... any insight would be much appreciated!
>

> Jen

Seeing only "not AA" and "not BB" but no "AA" or "BB" seems really unusual.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] New markers addition
messages.body_plain:
It would be helpful to have some context for your question.

Do you have genotype data on a cross, with a known genetic map for most of the markers, but a few new markers with unknown position?

In that case, I would assign the new markers to some arbitrary linkage group (e.g., "un") in the data file, and then use the function tryallpositions() for each such marker, one at a time, to estimate their position relative to the other markers.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] dominant markers and formLinkageGroups()
messages.body_plain:
If you use ripple() with method="likelihood", it uses an iterative algorithm to estimate inter-marker distances and evaluate the likelihood for a marker order.

There's a tolerance value to check for convergence (that the estimates haven't changed from one iteration to the next) plus some maximum number of iterations.  If the algorithm reaches the maximum number of iterations with the estimates still changing by more than the tolerance value at each iteration, that warning appears.

You can probably ignore it, because the likelihood for each order can be reasonably well established even without reaching convergence.

karl

messages.body_plain:
One possible reason for the convergence messages is that with dominant markers there is reduced information on recombination relative to co-dominant markers.  For example, if you have a AA/notAA dominant marker next to a co-dominant marker, individuals who are BB for the co-dominant marker are essentially non-informative when the recombination fraction is small.  If you have a AA/notAA marker next to a BB/notBB marker, you have almost no information about recombination between them unless the recombination fraction is large.

Saunak

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] adjusted p-values
messages.body_plain:
You need to consider the correlations among the phenotypes, and you should perform the permutation tests in a way that they are linked across phenotypes: that you permute the rows of the phenotype matrix relative to the rows of the genotype matrix.  This is what is done in R/qtl, as the default, if you do

  perms <- scanone(mycross, pheno=1:nphe(mycross), n.perm=1000, method="hk")

Then you can use the permutation results to calculate the expected value that you're looking for: count the number of phenotypes exceeding the threshold in each permutation replicate, and then average across replicates.

karl

Currently I am thinking about running the missing value thresholds again, however at a artificial high level to drop further markers, however that seems to be a bit dodgy and most likely will not results in similar spacing.

There's a function pickMarkerSubset() for choosing a subset of markers with no two markers within some fixed distance of each other.

For example, we might simulate a very-saturated map:

 map <- sim.map(rep(100, 10), n.mar=1001, anchor.tel <http://anchor.tel>=TRUE, include.x=FALSE)

And then simulate a cross with that map:

 x <- sim.cross(map, n.ind=100)
 totmar(x)

If I wanted to thin out the markers so that adjacent markers were always > 1 cM apart, I would do:

  map <- pull.map(x)
  markers2keep <- lapply(map, pickMarkerSubset, min.distance=1)
  xsub <- pull.markers(x, unlist(markers2keep))
  totmar(xsub)

karl

messages.body_plain:
There's something wrong with the format of the 'output' object.  It doesn't seem to be straight scanone output.

It may be a list of scanone objects, in which case you can combine them into one object through the following:

  for(i in 2:length(output)) output[[1]] <- cbind(output[[1]], output[[i]])
  output <- output[[1]]

For summary.scanone with multiple LOD curves, I prefer format="tabByChr" and format="tabByCol"; you might try those.

karl
